title: System Design Core Concepts — Quiz
subtitle: 40 questions across Networking, Caching, Sharding, CAP Theorem, and more. Shuffled each attempt.

questions.q: For most system design interviews, what is the default communication protocol you should use?
opts: gRPC over HTTP/2
WebSockets
HTTP over TCP
Server-Sent Events
questions.exp: HTTP over TCP is the well-understood default that works everywhere and handles 90% of use cases. Only deviate with a specific reason.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Server-Sent Events (SSE) and WebSockets?
opts: SSE is faster than WebSockets
SSE is unidirectional (server pushes to client); WebSockets are bidirectional
WebSockets only work within a data center
SSE requires a special load balancer
questions.exp: SSE opens an HTTP connection and the server pushes data down it — the client can't send back over the same connection. WebSockets support true two-way messaging.

questions.q: When is it appropriate to use WebSockets instead of SSE?
opts: Any time real-time updates are mentioned
When you need live scores or notifications
When clients need to push data back to the server frequently
When performance is more critical than simplicity
questions.exp: WebSockets are necessary only when clients genuinely need to send data back to the server frequently (e.g. chat, live collaboration). SSE is simpler and sufficient for one-way pushes.

questions.q: Why can't WebSocket connections be placed behind a standard load balancer without special consideration?
opts: WebSockets use a different port than HTTP
They are stateful persistent connections that must be maintained by the same server
WebSockets don't support TLS
Standard load balancers can't handle binary data
questions.exp: WebSockets (and SSE) are stateful connections. A standard L7 load balancer would break the persistent connection. You need L4 balancing or sticky sessions.

questions.q: What type of load balancer is typically required when dealing with WebSocket connections?
opts: Layer 7, because it inspects HTTP content
Layer 4, because it maintains a persistent TCP connection
DNS-based load balancing
Anycast load balancing
questions.exp: WebSockets require Layer 4 (TCP-level) load balancing because you're maintaining a persistent TCP connection, not individual HTTP requests.

questions.q: Why is gRPC not used for public-facing APIs?
opts: gRPC is too slow for public traffic
Browsers don't natively support gRPC
gRPC doesn't support authentication
gRPC only works within a single data center
questions.exp: Browsers don't natively support gRPC. gRPC-Web exists as a workaround but requires a proxy and has limitations. The common pattern is REST externally, gRPC internally.

questions.q: What is the minimum latency of a request from New York to London, regardless of processing time?
opts: Around 5ms
Around 20ms
Around 80ms
Around 200ms
questions.exp: A transatlantic request has roughly 80ms minimum latency just from the speed of light through fiber optic cables, before any processing occurs.

questions.q: What pagination approach works better for real-time data where new items are frequently added?
opts: Offset-based pagination
Cursor-based pagination
Page-number pagination
Keyset pagination
questions.exp: Cursor-based pagination handles real-time data better because it uses a stable pointer into the dataset, unaffected by new items being inserted (which would shift offset-based pages).

questions.q: What is a common mistake candidates make during the API design phase of a system design interview?
opts: Using REST instead of GraphQL
Spending too much time designing APIs instead of moving to architectural problems
Not specifying authentication
Forgetting to mention rate limiting
questions.exp: Spending too long on API design is a common trap. You should sketch 4-5 key endpoints in a couple of minutes and move on to the harder architectural questions.

questions.q: What authentication mechanism is recommended for service-to-service calls?
opts: JWT tokens
OAuth 2.0
API keys
Session cookies
questions.exp: JWT tokens are recommended for user sessions; API keys are the go-to for service-to-service calls.

questions.q: What is normalization in the context of relational databases?
opts: Adding indexes to frequently queried columns
Splitting data across tables to avoid duplication
Copying data into multiple tables for faster reads
Partitioning data across multiple servers
questions.exp: Normalization splits data across tables to avoid duplication. Each piece of data is stored once and referenced by ID, keeping data consistent but requiring joins to assemble complete records.

questions.q: What is the main downside of denormalization?
opts: It makes reads slower
It increases storage costs dramatically
Updates become complex — you must update the same data in multiple places
It prevents the use of indexes
questions.exp: Denormalization duplicates data to avoid joins, making reads faster. But when data changes, you must update every copy — e.g. a username stored in thousands of order records.

questions.q: What is the recommended default approach to data modeling in a system design interview?
opts: Start with a denormalized model for best read performance
Start normalized and denormalize specific hot paths only if read performance issues arise
Use NoSQL by default to avoid schema constraints
Shard from the beginning to future-proof the design
questions.exp: Start normalized, then selectively denormalize hot paths when you can justify it. This shows you understand the tradeoffs rather than blindly applying techniques.

questions.q: In DynamoDB, what determines how efficiently a query runs?
opts: The number of indexes defined
Whether the query uses a join
Whether the access pattern matches the partition key and sort key design
The size of the items being stored
questions.exp: DynamoDB requires you to design your partition key and sort key around your access patterns upfront. Queries that don't match the key design require expensive full table scans.

questions.q: When does a relational database like Postgres excel over NoSQL?
opts: When you need to scale horizontally across many servers
When your data structure changes very frequently
When you have structured data with clear relationships and need strong consistency
When you need schema-less flexible documents
questions.exp: Relational databases shine with structured, relational data requiring strong consistency, complex queries (SQL), transactions, and foreign key constraints.

questions.q: Without an index on an email column in a table with 10 million users, how does the database find a user by email?
opts: It uses a hash lookup
It scans every single row in the table
It queries a secondary index automatically
It caches the result from a previous query
questions.exp: Without an index, the database must perform a full table scan — checking every one of the 10 million rows. An index lets it jump directly to the matching row.

questions.q: What type of index supports both exact lookups AND range queries?
opts: Hash index
Full-text index
B-tree index
Geospatial index
questions.exp: B-tree indexes keep data sorted in a tree structure, supporting both exact matches and range queries (e.g. all orders between date A and date B). Hash indexes only support exact matches.

questions.q: What is the role of change data capture (CDC) when syncing to an external search index like Elasticsearch?
opts: It prevents stale data from ever appearing in the search index
It streams changes from the primary database to the search index, causing a small lag
It replaces the primary database with the search index
It validates data consistency between the two systems
questions.exp: CDC streams changes from the primary DB to Elasticsearch. This means the search index lags slightly behind the primary — but for search use cases, that small staleness is almost always acceptable.

questions.q: When would you use a compound index?
opts: When you only ever query by a single column
When you have composite queries filtering on multiple columns simultaneously
When you need full-text search capabilities
When your table has more than 1 million rows
questions.exp: Compound indexes cover queries that filter on multiple columns at once — e.g. finding events in a specific city on a specific date requires an index on both city and date.

questions.q: What is the performance difference between a Redis cache hit and a typical database query?
opts: Cache is about 2x faster
Cache is about 5x faster
Cache is about 20-50x faster
They are roughly the same speed
questions.exp: A Redis cache hit takes ~1ms vs 20-50ms for a typical DB query — a 20-50x speedup that matters enormously at millions of requests per second.

questions.q: Describe the cache-aside pattern (the most common caching strategy).
opts: Write to cache first, then asynchronously write to DB
Check cache first; on miss, query DB, store result in cache with TTL, return result
Always write to both cache and DB simultaneously
Pre-populate the cache with all data at startup
questions.exp: Cache-aside: check cache → if hit, return it. If miss, query the DB, store result in cache with a TTL, and return it. Simple and effective for read-heavy systems.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede?
opts: When the cache fills up and starts evicting entries rapidly
When Redis goes down and every request suddenly hits the database, potentially taking down the system
When multiple clients write conflicting data to the cache simultaneously
When cache TTLs are set too short, causing frequent misses
questions.exp: A cache stampede occurs when the cache fails and the full request load suddenly hits the database, which may not be sized to handle it — potentially causing a full system outage.

questions.q: What data is best suited for caching?
opts: Data that changes on every request
Data that is written more often than read
Data that is read frequently and doesn't change often
All data to minimize database load
questions.exp: Cache data that is read frequently and changes rarely. Caching data that changes on every request just adds latency and complexity for zero benefit.

questions.q: What is CDN caching primarily used for, as distinct from Redis caching?
opts: Storing user session data
Caching database query results near the application server
Serving static assets like images, videos, and JS files from edge locations near users
Caching microservice responses internally
questions.exp: CDN caching serves static assets (images, videos, JS) from geographically distributed edge servers near users. Redis handles application data. They serve different purposes.

questions.q: What is the primary reason to introduce sharding into a system?
opts: To improve read latency on a single server
To support full-text search
To split data across multiple independent servers when a single DB is no longer sufficient
To enable strong consistency across replicas
questions.exp: Sharding splits data across multiple independent servers when you've hit limits on storage, write throughput, or read throughput that replicas can't address.

questions.q: What is the most important decision when implementing sharding?
opts: Whether to use SQL or NoSQL
Choosing the shard key — it determines data distribution and query performance
Choosing between L4 and L7 load balancers
Selecting the replication factor
questions.exp: The shard key determines how data is distributed and affects everything — which queries are fast (single-shard) and which are slow (cross-shard scatter-gather).

questions.q: What is a hot spot in the context of database sharding?
opts: A shard that stores data at a higher temperature for faster access
When one shard receives disproportionately more traffic than others
A network bottleneck between shards
A shard that has run out of storage space
questions.exp: A hot spot occurs when one shard gets far more traffic than others — e.g. Taylor Swift's shard getting hammered while others sit idle — defeating the purpose of sharding.

questions.q: What is the biggest mistake candidates make when proposing sharding?
opts: Choosing a poor shard key
Proposing sharding too early, before the numbers justify it
Using hash-based instead of range-based sharding
Not considering cross-shard transactions
questions.exp: Sharding too early is the most common mistake. A well-tuned single database with read replicas handles far more than most candidates think. Do the capacity math first.

questions.q: Why are cross-shard transactions problematic?
opts: They require a special network protocol
They become nearly impossible and require distributed transactions or sagas, which are complex and slow
They prevent the use of indexes on sharded data
They require all shards to be on the same physical machine
questions.exp: When a transaction touches data on multiple shards, you need distributed transactions or saga patterns — both complex and slow. Good shard boundaries avoid cross-shard transactions.

questions.q: What problem does consistent hashing solve that simple modulo hashing does not?
opts: It distributes data more evenly across servers
It allows servers to be added or removed with minimal data movement
It supports range queries across distributed nodes
It prevents hot spots in distributed caches
questions.exp: With simple modulo hashing, adding/removing one server remaps nearly all keys. Consistent hashing only remaps the fraction of keys belonging to the affected range — roughly 1/N keys.

questions.q: How does consistent hashing work at a high level?
opts: It assigns each server a fixed numeric range of keys
Both servers and keys are hashed onto a virtual ring; each key belongs to the next server clockwise
It maintains a directory of key-to-server mappings updated on each change
It uses a leader server to coordinate which server holds each key
questions.exp: Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a virtual ring. A key belongs to the next server clockwise from its position. Adding/removing a server only affects neighboring keys.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of data must move when adding one server to a 10-server cluster using simple modulo hashing?
opts: About 10%
About 50%
About 90%
About 1%
questions.exp: With simple modulo hashing, adding one server changes N from 10 to 11, so hash(key) % N changes for ~90% of keys — nearly all data must move. Consistent hashing only moves ~10%.

questions.q: In an interview, when is it most relevant to bring up consistent hashing?
opts: When designing the API layer
When discussing elastic scaling of cache nodes or database shards
When choosing between SQL and NoSQL
When implementing rate limiting
questions.exp: Consistent hashing is most relevant when discussing elastic scaling — adding/removing cache nodes or DB shards — as the mechanism that avoids massive data movement.

questions.q: The CAP theorem says you can only have two of three properties. In practice, since network partitions are unavoidable, what is the real choice?
opts: Between performance and durability
Between consistency and availability
Between latency and throughput
Between sharding and replication
questions.exp: Since partition tolerance is a requirement in any distributed system (partitions will happen), the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition.

questions.q: What does an availability-favoring system do during a network partition?
opts: Refuses to serve requests until the partition heals
Serves requests from all nodes even if data may be temporarily inconsistent across them
Elects a leader node to serve all requests
Redirects all traffic to a single replica
questions.exp: An availability-favoring system keeps serving requests on all nodes during a partition. Users always get a response, but different nodes may temporarily have different data.

questions.q: What is eventual consistency?
opts: A consistency model where reads always return the most recent write
A model where the system guarantees all nodes will converge to the same state given enough time without new updates
A model that makes no guarantees about data convergence
Strong consistency with a slight delay
questions.exp: Eventual consistency guarantees that all nodes will eventually converge to the same state if no new updates are made — different from weak consistency, which makes no convergence guarantee.

questions.q: Which of these systems genuinely requires strong consistency rather than eventual consistency?
opts: Social media feeds
Video recommendation systems
Inventory counts in an e-commerce system to prevent overselling
Analytics dashboards
questions.exp: Inventory systems need accurate counts — selling a product you don't have costs real money. Social feeds, recommendations, and analytics can tolerate briefly stale data.

questions.q: What does the PACELC theorem add to CAP theorem's model?
opts: It adds a fifth property: partition tolerance in all conditions
During normal (non-partition) operation, there is still a tradeoff between latency and consistency
It shows that availability and consistency are never truly in conflict
It replaces CAP theorem with a more accurate model
questions.exp: PACELC: during a Partition choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal ops) choose Latency or Consistency. Strong consistency always adds latency because nodes must coordinate before responding.

questions.q: Approximately how many operations per second can a single Redis instance handle?
opts: Around 1,000
Around 10,000
Around 100,000+
questions.exp: A single Redis instance handles hundreds of thousands of operations per second. Most candidates underestimate modern hardware and propose caching layers unnecessarily early.

questions.q: At roughly what storage size does a single Postgres instance become a candidate for sharding?
opts: 500 GB
Tens to hundreds of terabytes
10 TB
100 GB
questions.exp: A single Postgres instance handles a few terabytes comfortably. You don't need sharding until you're hitting tens or hundreds of terabytes. Proposing sharding at 500GB adds massive unnecessary complexity.

questions.q: What is the approximate latency for a network call within a single data center?
opts: Nanoseconds
Microseconds
1–10 milliseconds
100+ milliseconds
questions.exp: Intra-datacenter network calls take 1-10ms. Memory access is nanoseconds, SSD reads are microseconds, and cross-continent calls are tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

questions.q: When should you perform back-of-the-envelope capacity calculations in a system design interview?
opts: Always at the very start of the interview
Never — interviewers don't care about numbers
When you need to make a specific decision, like whether to shard or whether Redis can handle the load
Only when the interviewer explicitly asks for them
questions.exp: Do the math when it's decision-relevant — 'should I shard? can a single Redis handle this?' — not as a ritual at the start. Interviewers want to see you think through numbers in context.
